newsitem.title: USA: Mexican ex-official says U.S. suit aims to quiet him.
newsitem.headline: Mexican ex-official says U.S. suit aims to quiet him.

text.p: A former Mexican official accused of taking money from drug traffickers has argued in court papers that an upcoming civil trial to confiscate his money is an attempt by the U.S. and Mexican governments to shut him up, presumably about high-level corruption in Mexico.

Mario Ruiz Massieu, once a Mexican deputy attorney general and high-ranking anti-drug official, has also said the legal action, in which U.S. prosecutors will try to seize $9 million he holds in a Houston bank, is the product of a U.S. misunderstanding of Mexican culture. The trial is scheduled to start on March 10 in federal court.
Prosecutors say the money Ruiz Massieu stashed in Texas Commerce Bank starting in 1992 was part of a fortune he amassed from bribes paid by drug traffickers seeking protection.

But in a response to government interrogatories filed last week, Ruiz Massieu said "the forfeiture action is part of an effort by the United States to assist the Mexican government in silencing (him)." The complaint, he said, has no legal or factual basis and is brought for the purpose of harassment."

Two years ago Ruiz Massieu accused old-guard elements in Mexico's long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) of ordering the September 1994 assassination of his brother Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu, then PRI general secretary.

Ruiz Massieu made the accusations after leading a government investigation into his brother's death. But shortly thereafter, in March 1995, he fled Mexico amid charges he had in fact covered up for the man who allegedly masterminded Jose Francisco's shooting -- Raul Salinas, the jailed brother of former Mexican President Carlos Salinas de Gortari.

After leaving Mexico, Ruiz Massieu was arrested in the Newark, New Jersey airport on charges he failed to tell U.S. Customs he was carrying $46,000 in cash. He is currently out on bond and living in New Jersey. Repeated attempts to have him sent back to Mexico to face charges have been rejected by U.S. judges for lack of proof.

According to the Mexican news magazine Proceso, the U.S. government now has evidence showing that Ruiz Massieu and Raul Salinas were part of a larger conspiracy involving top political figures who collected hundreds of millions of dollars in payoffs from drug traffickers. A government witness has allegedly testified that the conspiracy was headed by Raul Salinas Lozano, the father of the Salinas brothers.

The Salinas family has denied the accusations. It now appears likely that Raul Salinas has been or will be questioned by lawyers in the case. Court records filed on Thursday included a motion by the defence to interview him and on Saturday, Mexico City daily La Jornada said Salinas, in jail now for two years but still not tried for supposedly ordering the killing of Jose Francisco and financial misconduct, offered to give testimony to exonerate Ruiz Massieu.

Ruiz Massieu has also denied the charges, saying the money in the Texas bank came from his family and his own hefty earnings as a Mexican official. In depositions, he said his family pooled the $9 million to place in the Texas bank to protect it from economic uncertainty in Mexico.
He said it was common for wealthy Mexicans to put their money in the U.S. banks, and to do it as a family, giving all authority to one person with no written agreements.
"It was money that was given to me as my property, which is the way in which a family functions in Mexico, and perhaps this may appear strange here," Ruiz Massieu said.
Affidavits from his father and another brother, Arturo, both of whom gave depositions here last week, back him up, saying the deal followed the "cultural traditions of Mexico."
